\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The method and its reputation}

The probabilistic method, inaugurated by Erd\H{o}s in 1947, proves that an object with property $P$ exists by placing a probability measure on a space of candidates and showing $\Prob[P] > 0$. It is universally described as \emph{non-constructive}. This description conflates two things.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Finitary non-constructivity.} The proof uses averaging rather than explicit construction. This is a feature of the presentation: if the sample space is finite, ``positive probability'' asserts that a certain finite set is non-empty, and the argument reduces to a comparison of integers.
  \item \textbf{Computational non-constructivity.} The implied search is exponential and no efficient algorithm is known. This obstruction is real, and for Ramsey colourings it remains open.
\end{itemize}

This paper is a systematic study of the first phenomenon: for each classical application we exhibit a finitary avatar of the probabilistic argument and, wherever possible, an explicit algorithm.

\subsection{Notation}

$G=(V,E)$ is a finite simple graph, $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$; $\deg(v)$ is the degree of $v$, $\Delta$ the maximum degree, $\alpha(G)$ the independence number, $\omega(G)$ the clique number, $G^{c}$ the complement. $G$ is \emph{$K_j$-free} if it has no clique on $j$ vertices. $T(n,r)$ is the Tur\'an graph: $V$ split into $r$ classes of sizes as equal as possible, with two vertices adjacent iff they lie in different classes. $R(k,k)$ is the diagonal Ramsey number.

\section{Ramsey's lower bound as an inequality between integers}

\subsection{Colourings as subsets}

Let $\Pairs(n)$ be the set of two-element subsets of $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, so $|\Pairs(n)|=\binom n2$; for $K\subseteq\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ let $\Pairs(K)$ be the two-element subsets of $K$.

\begin{definition}
A \emph{two-colouring} of $K_n$ is a subset $S\subseteq\Pairs(n)$ (the red edges). There are exactly $2^{\binom n2}$ colourings. $S$ is \emph{monochromatic on} $K$ if $\Pairs(K)\subseteq S$ or $\Pairs(K)\cap S=\varnothing$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Supersets and disjoint sets]\label{lem:count}
For finite sets $T\subseteq E$, the number of subsets of $E$ containing $T$ is $2^{|E|-|T|}$, and the number of subsets of $E$ disjoint from $T$ is also $2^{|E|-|T|}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The maps $S\mapsto S\setminus T$ and $S\mapsto S$ are bijections onto the power set of $E\setminus T$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:badone}
For $|K|=k$, the number of colourings monochromatic on $K$ is at most $2\cdot2^{\binom n2-\binom k2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Split into colourings containing $\Pairs(K)$ and colourings disjoint from it, and apply Lemma~\ref{lem:count} with $E=\Pairs(n)$, $T=\Pairs(K)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Union bound]\label{lem:union}
The number of colourings monochromatic on \emph{some} $k$-set is at most $\binom nk\cdot2\cdot2^{\binom n2-\binom k2}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The family is a union of $\binom nk$ families as in Lemma~\ref{lem:badone}, and the cardinality of a union of finite sets is at most the sum of the cardinalities.
\end{proof}

Lemma~\ref{lem:union} is the counting shadow of the probabilistic union bound; no measure is involved.

\subsection{The expectation argument, de-randomised}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:goodcol}
If $k\le n$ and $2\binom nk<2^{\binom k2}$, then some colouring of $K_n$ is monochromatic on no $k$-set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:union} the bad colourings number at most $\binom nk\,2\,2^{\binom n2-\binom k2}$; multiplying the hypothesis by $2^{\binom n2-\binom k2}$ shows this is strictly less than $2^{\binom n2}$, the total. A proper subfamily of a finite family is not all of it.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:graphform}
Under the hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:goodcol} there is a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices with $G$ and $G^{c}$ both $K_k$-free.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $G$ have the red pairs of a good colouring as edges. A $k$-clique of $G$ (resp.\ of $G^{c}$) is a $k$-set all of whose pairs are red (resp.\ blue), hence monochromatic; both are excluded.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The arithmetic engine}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:arith}
For every $k\ge3$, $2^{k+2}<(k!)^2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Induction. Base $k=3$: $32<36$. Step: the left side is multiplied by $2$, the right by $(k+1)^2\ge16$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:hyp}
If $k\ge3$ and $n^2\le2^k$, then $2\binom nk<2^{\binom k2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Bound $\binom nk\le n^k/k!$ and $n^k\le 2^{k^2/2}$, and note $\binom k2=k^2/2-k/2$; the deficit $2^{k/2}$ is absorbed by $k!/2>2^{k/2}$, which is Theorem~\ref{thm:arith}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Erd\H{o}s, 1947, de-randomised]
If $3\le k\le n$ and $n^2\le2^k$ (i.e.\ $n\le2^{k/2}$), then there is a graph on $n$ vertices such that neither it nor its complement contains a $K_k$. Consequently, if every graph on $m$ vertices contains a clique or independent set of size $k$, then $m>n$; in particular $R(k,k)>2^{k/2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:hyp} then Theorem~\ref{thm:graphform}; Ramsey witnesses restrict along injections, so a witness on $n$ vertices rules out the Ramsey property for every $m\le n$.
\end{proof}

\section{The deletion method}

For a colouring $S$ let $\mono_k(S)$ be the number of $k$-sets on which $S$ is monochromatic.

\begin{lemma}[Double count]\label{lem:double}
$\sum_{S}\mono_k(S)=\sum_{|K|=k}\#\{S: S\text{ monochromatic on }K\}\le\binom nk\cdot2\cdot2^{\binom n2-\binom k2}$, the sums ranging over all colourings and all $k$-subsets respectively.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Both sides count pairs $(S,K)$ with $S$ monochromatic on $K$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:badone}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Averaging]\label{thm:avg}
If $k\le n$ and $2\binom nk<(t+1)2^{\binom k2}$, then some colouring $S$ has $\mono_k(S)\le t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise the left side of Lemma~\ref{lem:double} is at least $(t+1)2^{\binom n2}$, contradicting the hypothesis multiplied by $2^{\binom n2-\binom k2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Minimum-element transversal]\label{lem:trans}
Let $B$ be a finite family of non-empty subsets of a linearly ordered finite set and let $T=\{\min K: K\in B\}$. Then $|T|\le|B|$ and $T\cap K\neq\varnothing$ for all $K\in B$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$T$ is the image of $B$ under $\min$, hence no larger, and $\min K\in T\cap K$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Deletion method]\label{thm:del}
If $1\le k\le n$ and $2\binom nk<(t+1)2^{\binom k2}$, then there is a graph $G$ on $n-t$ vertices with $G$ and $G^{c}$ both $K_k$-free; hence $R(k,k)>n-t$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take $S$ with $\mono_k(S)\le t$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:avg}) and let $B$ be its family of bad $k$-sets. Lemma~\ref{lem:trans} gives $T$ with $|T|\le t$ meeting every member of $B$. Put $W=V\setminus T$, so $|W|\ge n-t$; no $k$-subset of $W$ is monochromatic, since such a set would lie in $B$ and hence meet $T$. Pull the colouring back along an order-embedding of $\{0,\dots,n-t-1\}$ into $W$: cliques of the pull-back and of its complement would give monochromatic $k$-subsets of $W$.
\end{proof}

Taking $t=0$ recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:graphform}, so the deletion bound is a strict generalisation.

\begin{proposition}[An exact gain at $k=6$]
$2\binom{19}{6}=54264<65536=2\cdot2^{\binom62}$, so Theorem~\ref{thm:del} with $n=19$, $t=1$ produces a graph on $18$ vertices with $G$, $G^{c}$ both $K_6$-free, i.e.\ $R(6,6)>18$. The union bound is unavailable at $n=18$: $2\binom{18}{6}=37128\ge32768=2^{\binom62}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Erd\H{o}s--Szekeres and the sandwich]
If a vertex set has at least $\binom{s+t}{s}$ elements, every graph on it contains a clique of size $s+1$ or an independent set of size $t+1$. Since $\binom{2m}{m}\le4^m$, we get $R(k,k)\le4^{k-1}$, and hence for $k\ge3$
\[
2^{k/2}<R(k,k)\le4^{k-1}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $s+t$ using $\binom{s+t}{s}=\binom{s+t-1}{s-1}+\binom{s+t-1}{s}$: for a fixed vertex $v$, its neighbourhood or its non-neighbourhood is large enough for the induction hypothesis, and $v$ extends the resulting clique or independent set.
\end{proof}

\section{Caro--Wei by greedy deletion}

\begin{definition}
For $t\subseteq V$ let $\deg_t(v)=|\{w\in t: v\sim w\}|$, the degree of $v$ measured inside $t$; thus $\deg_V=\deg$ and $t'\subseteq t$ implies $\deg_{t'}\le\deg_t$. The \emph{closed neighbourhood of $v$ inside $t$} is $B_t(v)=\{v\}\cup\{w\in t: v\sim w\}$; for $v\in t$ we have $B_t(v)\subseteq t$ and $|B_t(v)|=\deg_t(v)+1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Relative Caro--Wei]\label{thm:relcw}
For every $t\subseteq V$ there is an independent set $s\subseteq t$ with
\[
\sum_{v\in t}\frac{1}{\deg_t(v)+1}\;\le\;|s|.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Strong induction on $|t|$; the empty case is trivial. Choose $v\in t$ minimising $\deg_t$, set $d=\deg_t(v)$ and $B=B_t(v)$, so $|B|=d+1$ and $B\subseteq t$. Since $v\notin t\setminus B$, the set $t\setminus B$ is a proper subset of $t$; the induction hypothesis gives an independent $s'\subseteq t\setminus B$ with $\sum_{u\in t\setminus B}1/(\deg_{t\setminus B}(u)+1)\le|s'|$.

\emph{Independence.} Every $u\in s'$ lies outside $B$, hence $u\neq v$ and $u\not\sim v$; non-adjacency is symmetric, so $s:=\{v\}\cup s'$ is independent, and $|s|=|s'|+1$.

\emph{Counting.} Split the sum over $t$ into the parts over $B$ and over $t\setminus B$. For $u\in B$, minimality gives $\deg_t(u)\ge d$, so the $B$-block contributes at most $|B|/(d+1)=1$. For $u\in t\setminus B$, monotonicity gives $\deg_{t\setminus B}(u)\le\deg_t(u)$, so the remaining block is at most $|s'|$. The total is at most $|s'|+1=|s|$.
\end{proof}

The proof is literally the greedy algorithm: pick a minimum-degree vertex, output it, delete its closed neighbourhood, recurse.

\begin{theorem}[Caro--Wei]\label{thm:cw}
$\displaystyle \sum_{v\in V}\frac{1}{\deg(v)+1}\le\alpha(G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:maxdeg}
$\alpha(G)\ge n/(\Delta+1)$; equivalently $n\le\alpha(G)(\Delta+1)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Sedrakyan / Cauchy--Schwarz]\label{lem:sed}
For positive reals $a_1,\dots,a_n$, $\sum_i 1/a_i\ge n^2/\sum_i a_i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{corollary}[Tur\'an's independence bound]
$\alpha(G)\ge n^2/(2m+n)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:sed} with $a_v=\deg(v)+1$, using $\sum_v\deg(v)=2m$, and then Theorem~\ref{thm:cw}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Tur\'an's theorem, greedy proof]\label{thm:turan}
Let $r\ge1$ and let $G$ be a $K_{r+1}$-free graph on a finite vertex set of size $n$. Then
\[
m\;\le\;\Bigl(1-\frac1r\Bigr)\frac{n^2}{2}.
\]
No divisibility hypothesis and no structural assumption on the vertex set are required.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $n=0$ both sides vanish. Otherwise $\deg_{G^{c}}(v)=n-1-\deg_G(v)$, so $\sum_v(\deg_{G^{c}}(v)+1)=n^2-2m$, which is positive as a sum of positive terms. Lemma~\ref{lem:sed} with $a_v=\deg_{G^{c}}(v)+1$, Caro--Wei on $G^{c}$, and $\alpha(G^{c})=\omega(G)\le r$ give
\[
\frac{n^2}{n^2-2m}\;\le\;\sum_v\frac{1}{\deg_{G^{c}}(v)+1}\;\le\;\alpha(G^{c})\;\le\;r,
\]
whence $n^2\le r(n^2-2m)$, i.e.\ $2rm\le(r-1)n^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Sharpness]
For $r=2$, $n=4$ the four-cycle $T(4,2)$ is triangle-free with exactly $4$ edges, while $(1-\tfrac12)\cdot\tfrac{16}{2}=4$; the constant cannot be improved. Its maximum degree is $2$, so Corollary~\ref{cor:maxdeg} gives only $4/3$ while $\alpha=2$: the loss is the convexity slack in Lemma~\ref{lem:sed}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{theorem}[Triangle-free graphs and $R(3,k+1)>k^2$]
If $G$ is triangle-free then $\Delta\le\alpha(G)$ (neighbourhoods are independent), hence $n\le\alpha(G)(\alpha(G)+1)$, i.e.\ $\alpha(G)\ge\sqrt n-1$. Consequently every graph on more than $k(k+1)$ vertices contains a triangle or an independent set of size $k+1$.
\end{theorem}

\section{The Tur\'an graph, counted exactly}

Let $T(n,r)$ have vertex set $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ with $u\sim v$ iff $u\not\equiv v\pmod r$.

\begin{lemma}[Class sizes]\label{lem:classes}
Write $n=qr+s$ with $s=n\bmod r$, $0\le s<r$. Class $i$ has $q+1$ elements if $i<s$ and $q$ otherwise, so $\sum_{i<r}|C_i|^2=s(q+1)^2+(r-s)q^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Complete multipartite count]\label{lem:mp}
For any partition of $n$ vertices into classes $C_i$, the complete multipartite graph satisfies $2e+\sum_i|C_i|^2=n^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Count ordered pairs of vertices: $n^2$ in total, of which $\sum_i|C_i|^2$ lie inside a class and the remaining $2e$ are the two orientations of the edges.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact Tur\'an edge identity]\label{thm:ident}
For all $n$ and all $r\ge1$, with $s=n\bmod r$,
\[
2r\,e\bigl(T(n,r)\bigr)+s(r-s)=(r-1)\,n^2 .
\]
The identity is subtraction-free over the natural numbers, and $s(r-s)=0$ exactly when $r\mid n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Substitute Lemma~\ref{lem:classes} into Lemma~\ref{lem:mp} and expand with $n=qr+s$: from $s(q+1)^2+(r-s)q^2=rq^2+2qs+s$ and $n^2=(qr+s)^2$ one obtains $2r\,e=(r-1)n^2-s(r-s)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$e(T(n,r))=\bigl(1-\tfrac1r\bigr)\tfrac{n^2}{2}-\tfrac{s(r-s)}{2r}$, and equality with the clean value $\bigl(1-\tfrac1r\bigr)\tfrac{n^2}{2}$ holds if and only if $r\mid n$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Tur\'an's theorem, exactly]\label{thm:exact}
For every $n$ and every $r\ge1$,
\[
\ex(n,K_{r+1})=\frac{(r-1)n^2-s(r-s)}{2r},\qquad s=n\bmod r,
\]
attained by $T(n,r)$: that graph is $K_{r+1}$-free with this many edges, and every $K_{r+1}$-free graph on $n$ vertices has at most this many.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[The floor formula and where it fails]
For $r\ge1$, $e(T(n,r))=\bigl\lfloor(r-1)n^2/(2r)\bigr\rfloor$ if and only if $s(r-s)<2r$. At $n=12$, $r=8$ we have $s=4$ and $s(r-s)=16=2r$, so $e(T(12,8))=62$ while $\lfloor 7\cdot144/16\rfloor=63$: the commonly quoted floor formula for the extremal number is false in general. For every $r<8$ and every $n$ the floor formula is correct, so $r=8$ is the first failing modulus.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:ident}, $\lfloor(r-1)n^2/(2r)\rfloor=e(T(n,r))+\lfloor s(r-s)/(2r)\rfloor$, and the second term vanishes iff $s(r-s)<2r$. For $r\le7$ and $s+t=r$ one checks $st<2r$ over the finitely many cases.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[An integer-convexity route]
Among decompositions $n=c_0+\dots+c_{r-1}$ into natural numbers, $\sum_i c_i^2$ is minimised by the balanced one, so $r\sum_i c_i^2\ge n^2$. Hence a properly $r$-colourable graph with class sizes $c_i$ satisfies $2m+\sum_i c_i^2\le n^2$ and therefore $2rm\le(r-1)n^2$, with equality forcing balanced classes and complete multipartiteness.
\end{remark}

\section{The Lov\'asz Local Lemma in a finite weighted space}

\begin{definition}
A \emph{finite weighted probability space} is a finite set $\Omega$ with weights $w:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ summing to $1$; the probability of $E\subseteq\Omega$ is $\Prob(E)=\sum_{\omega\in E}w(\omega)$. For bad events $A_i$ indexed by a finite set $I$ and $S\subseteq I$ put $\Av(S)=\{\omega:\forall i\in S,\ \omega\notin A_i\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Core estimate]\label{thm:core}
Let $\Gamma:I\to\mathcal P(I)$ and $x:I\to[0,1)$. Assume the one-sided (lopsided) independence hypothesis: for all $i$ and all $S\subseteq I$ with $i\notin S$ and $S\cap\Gamma(i)=\varnothing$,
\[
\Prob\bigl(A_i\cap\Av(S)\bigr)\le\Prob(A_i)\,\Prob\bigl(\Av(S)\bigr),
\]
and the weight condition $\Prob(A_i)\le x_i\prod_{j\in\Gamma(i)}(1-x_j)$. Then for every $S\subseteq I$ and $i\notin S$,
\[
\Prob\bigl(A_i\cap\Av(S)\bigr)\le x_i\,\Prob\bigl(\Av(S)\bigr).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $|S|$, splitting $S=S_1\sqcup S_2$ with $S_1=S\cap\Gamma(i)$ and $S_2=S\setminus\Gamma(i)$. If $S_1=\varnothing$ the hypotheses finish directly. Otherwise bound the ``numerator'' $\Prob(A_i\cap\Av(S_2))\le\Prob(A_i)\Prob(\Av(S_2))$ by one-sided independence, and the ``denominator'' from below by $\prod_{j\in S_1}(1-x_j)\Prob(\Av(S_2))$, which is the induction hypothesis applied one index of $S_1$ at a time. The weight condition converts $\Prob(A_i)/\prod_{j\in S_1}(1-x_j)$ into $x_i$, since $S_1\subseteq\Gamma(i)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[General asymmetric lopsided Local Lemma]\label{thm:lll}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:core},
\[
\Prob\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in I}\overline{A_i}\Bigr)\;\ge\;\prod_{i\in I}(1-x_i)\;>\;0 .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Peel indices one at a time: Theorem~\ref{thm:core} gives $\Prob(\Av(S\cup\{i\}))\ge(1-x_i)\Prob(\Av(S))$, starting from $\Av(\varnothing)=\Omega$. Positivity holds since every $x_i<1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetric Local Lemma]\label{thm:sym}
Suppose $\Prob(A_i)\le p$ for all $i$, $|\Gamma(i)|\le d$ for all $i$, the one-sided independence hypothesis holds, $p\ge0$, and $e\,p\,(d+1)\le1$. Then some $\omega\in\Omega$ lies in no $A_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $D=\max(d,1)$ and $x_i=1/(D+1)$. Using $\bigl(D/(D+1)\bigr)^{D}\ge e^{-1}$ (a consequence of $1+x\le e^x$),
\[
x_i\prod_{j\in\Gamma(i)}(1-x_j)\ \ge\ \frac{1}{D+1}\Bigl(\frac{D}{D+1}\Bigr)^{d}\ \ge\ \frac{1}{e(d+1)}\ \ge\ p\ \ge\ \Prob(A_i),
\]
so Theorem~\ref{thm:lll} applies and the avoidance event has positive probability, hence is non-empty.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The existence proof is an algorithm]
Let $\operatorname{search}(A)$ enumerate $\Omega$ and return the first element of $\Av(I)$, or failure. It is sound (whatever it returns avoids all bad events) and, under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:lll} (in particular under $e\,p\,(d+1)\le1$), it never fails.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Soundness is immediate. For completeness, Theorem~\ref{thm:lll} gives $\Prob(\Av(I))>0$; a finite set of total weight $0$ is empty, so $\Av(I)\neq\varnothing$ and the enumeration finds a member.
\end{proof}

\section{MAX-CUT: averaging and local search}

For $S\subseteq V$ let $\cut(S)$ be the number of edges with exactly one endpoint in $S$.

\begin{theorem}[Exact averaging identity]
$\sum_{S\subseteq V}\cut(S)=2m\cdot2^{\,n-2}$; the average cut over all $2^n$ bipartitions is exactly $m/2$. Consequently some $S$ satisfies $m\le2\cut(S)$, and the exhaustive maximum satisfies $m\le2\maxcut(G)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For each of the $2m$ ordered adjacent pairs $(u,v)$, the subsets $S$ with $u\in S$, $v\notin S$ number $2^{n-2}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exchange identity]\label{thm:exch}
Let $\operatorname{flip}(S,v)$ move $v$ to the other side and let $c_S(v)$ count the neighbours of $v$ on the opposite side. Then
\[
\cut(\operatorname{flip}(S,v))+2c_S(v)=\cut(S)+\deg(v),
\]
i.e.\ flipping $v$ changes the cut by exactly $\deg(v)-2c_S(v)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Local optima are $2$-approximate, and local search terminates]
Call $S$ \emph{locally maximal} if no single-vertex flip increases the cut. Then $m\le2\cut(S)$. Moreover any strictly improving run $S_0,S_1,\dots$ has at most $m$ steps.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:exch} and local maximality give $\deg(v)\le2c_S(v)$ for all $v$; summing and using $\sum_v\deg(v)=2m$ and $\sum_v c_S(v)=2\cut(S)$ gives $2m\le4\cut(S)$. For termination, $\cut(S_i)\ge i$ by induction while $\cut(S_i)\le m$ always.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[MAX-CUT meets Tur\'an]
$\maxcut(K_n)=\lfloor n/2\rfloor\cdot\lceil n/2\rceil=e\bigl(T(n,2)\bigr)=\ex(n,K_3)$: the largest bipartite subgraph of $K_n$ is exactly the extremal triangle-free graph.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $K_n$, $\cut(S)=|S|(n-|S|)$, maximised at the balanced split, and $4\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lceil n/2\rceil+(n\bmod 2)=n^2$. Theorem~\ref{thm:ident} at $r=2$ reads $4e(T(n,2))+(n\bmod 2)=n^2$, the same identity.
\end{proof}

\section{Property B by the same counting}

\begin{theorem}[Erd\H{o}s, property B]
Let $H$ be a $k$-uniform hypergraph on a finite vertex set $V$; a two-colouring is a subset $S\subseteq V$, and an edge $E$ is monochromatic if $E\subseteq S$ or $E\cap S=\varnothing$. At most $|H|\cdot2\cdot2^{|V|-k}$ colourings make some edge monochromatic; hence if $|H|<2^{k-1}$ then $H$ has a two-colouring with no monochromatic edge.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:count} with $E:=V$ and $T:=$ an edge, then subadditivity of cardinality over the union across edges. Under $|H|<2^{k-1}$ the bad colourings number fewer than $2^{k-1}\cdot2^{|V|-k+1}=2^{|V|}$, the total.
\end{proof}

The point is methodological: the counting lemmas of Section~2 are the only input, transferred verbatim by changing the ground set from the pair set of $K_n$ to the vertex set of $H$.

\section{Discussion}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule
Result & Probabilistic proof & Finitary avatar & Effective? \\
\midrule
$R(k,k)>2^{k/2}$ & union bound & inequality between integer counts & search over $2^{\binom n2}$ \\
deletion bound & expectation & double count $+$ min-element transversal & search, then deletion \\
Caro--Wei & random order & minimum-degree greedy deletion & yes, near-linear \\
Tur\'an & none needed & exact count of $T(n,r)$ & closed formula \\
Local Lemma & Erd\H{o}s--Lov\'asz & same induction, finite weighted space & search over $\Omega$ \\
MAX-CUT & random bipartition & averaging / exchange identity & $\le m$ steps \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Two of the six are genuinely efficient, one is a closed formula, and three reduce to certified terminating searches. The residual difficulty in the probabilistic method is therefore computational rather than logical: ``positive probability'' in a finite space means ``non-empty'', and non-empty means a search terminates.

In three places the finitary treatment is quantitatively stronger. Tur\'an's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:turan}) holds with no divisibility hypothesis. The exact extremal number (Theorem~\ref{thm:exact}) refutes the folklore floor formula at $n=12$, $r=8$. And the deletion bound provably beats the union bound at $k=6$, with both sides evaluated exactly.

Methodologically, three lessons recur: \emph{relativise the induction} (Caro--Wei has no induction in absolute form but a three-line induction in relative form); \emph{avoid subtraction} (the Tur\'an identity is stated additively over the natural numbers, and specialises to both the real formula and the divisibility criterion); and \emph{reuse counting lemmas across settings} (Section~8 is nearly free given Section~2).

\section{Future work}

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Efficient constructive Local Lemma.} Carry out the entropy-compression / witness-tree analysis of the resampling algorithm, replacing the certified exhaustive search by an efficient one.
  \item \textbf{Second moment method.} Variance in a finite weighted space is again a finite sum; the natural first target is concentration of triangle counts in random graphs.
  \item \textbf{Ramsey lower bounds beyond deletion.} The Local Lemma gives $R(k,k)>\tfrac{\sqrt2}{e}k\,2^{k/2}(1+o(1))$; running it with the pair-set dependency graph would unify Sections 2, 3 and 6.
  \item \textbf{Sharper off-diagonal bounds.} We obtain $R(3,k+1)>k^2$; the truth is $\Theta(k^2/\log k)$, and Shearer's bound is a Caro--Wei refinement that should fit the greedy framework.
  \item \textbf{Hypergraph Tur\'an numbers.} The exact count of Section~5 is a complete-multipartite calculation; exact analogues for $j$-uniform hypergraphs are open even in simple cases.
  \item \textbf{Quantitative property B.} The union bound gives $m(k)\ge2^{k-1}$; deletion and Local Lemma refinements give $\Omega(2^k\sqrt{k/\log k})$, both of the type de-randomised here.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

Across five classical landmarks of the probabilistic method---Erd\H{o}s's Ramsey lower bound, the deletion method, Caro--Wei and its Tur\'an corollaries, the Lov\'asz Local Lemma, and MAX-CUT---the probability space is a convenience, not a necessity. Each argument has a finitary avatar that is a comparison of integers, a greedy algorithm, or a local search. What separates Caro--Wei (a linear-time greedy algorithm) from the Ramsey bound (a search over $2^{\binom n2}$ colourings) is not the presence or absence of randomness but the structure of the search space---and the whole of algorithmic combinatorics lives in that gap.

"""
The Probabilistic Method as Finite Counting — numerical demonstrations.

Every classical "random construction" below is replaced by an exact finite
computation: a comparison of integers, a greedy algorithm, or a local search.
Nothing in this file calls a random number generator.

Demonstrations
--------------
1. Erdos' Ramsey lower bound as an inequality between two integers, and the
   arithmetic engine  2^(k+2) < (k!)^2  for k >= 3.
2. The deletion method, and the verified gain over the union bound at k = 6
   (R(6,6) > 18, which the union bound cannot reach).
3. The Ramsey sandwich  2^(k/2) < R(k,k) <= 4^(k-1).
4. Caro-Wei by minimum-degree greedy deletion, compared with the bound
   sum_v 1/(deg v + 1) and with the exact independence number.
5. Turan's theorem: the exact edge identity 2 r e(T(n,r)) + s(r-s) = (r-1) n^2,
   the exact extremal number, and the failure of the floor formula at n=12, r=8.
6. MAX-CUT: the exact averaging identity, local search, and the identity
   maxcut(K_n) = e(T(n,2)).
7. The symmetric Lovasz Local Lemma in a finite weighted space, with the
   certified exhaustive search, on an explicit k-SAT instance.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import combinations, product
from math import comb, factorial, exp
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

Graph = Dict[int, Set[int]]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Small graph utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def make_graph(n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build an adjacency-set graph on vertices 0..n-1."""
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        if u == v:
            continue
        g[u].add(v)
        g[v].add(u)
    return g


def num_edges(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Number of edges of a simple graph."""
    return sum(len(nbrs) for nbrs in g.values()) // 2


def degrees(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Degree of every vertex."""
    return {v: len(nbrs) for v, nbrs in g.items()}


def turan_graph(n: int, r: int) -> Graph:
    """T(n, r): vertices 0..n-1, adjacent iff their residues mod r differ."""
    return make_graph(n, [(u, v) for u in range(n) for v in range(u + 1, n)
                          if u % r != v % r])


def complement(g: Graph) -> Graph:
    """The complement graph."""
    n = len(g)
    return make_graph(n, [(u, v) for u in range(n) for v in range(u + 1, n)
                          if v not in g[u]])


def independence_number(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Exact independence number by exhaustive search (small graphs only)."""
    n = len(g)
    best = 0
    for size in range(n, 0, -1):
        if size <= best:
            break
        for s in combinations(range(n), size):
            if all(v not in g[u] for u, v in combinations(s, 2)):
                return size
    return best


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Erdos' Ramsey lower bound as pure counting
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def union_bound_holds(n: int, k: int) -> bool:
    """The counting hypothesis 2*C(n,k) < 2^C(k,2) of the union bound."""
    return 2 * comb(n, k) < 2 ** comb(k, 2)


def bad_colourings_upper_bound(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Upper bound on the number of colourings monochromatic on some k-set."""
    return comb(n, k) * 2 * 2 ** (comb(n, 2) - comb(k, 2))


def arithmetic_engine(k: int) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """The inequality 2^(k+2) < (k!)^2, valid for every k >= 3."""
    return 2 ** (k + 2), factorial(k) ** 2, 2 ** (k + 2) < factorial(k) ** 2


def largest_n_by_union_bound(k: int) -> int:
    """Largest n for which the union bound certifies R(k,k) > n."""
    n = k
    while union_bound_holds(n + 1, k):
        n += 1
    return n


def demo_ramsey_counting() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("1. ERDOS' RAMSEY BOUND AS AN INEQUALITY BETWEEN TWO INTEGERS")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("A colouring of K_n is a subset of the pair set: 2^C(n,2) of them.")
    print("Bad colourings (monochromatic on some k-set) number at most")
    print("    C(n,k) * 2 * 2^(C(n,2)-C(k,2)).")
    print()
    print(f"{'k':>3} {'n':>4} {'bad <= ':>24} {'total = 2^C(n,2)':>26} {'good?':>7}")
    for k, n in [(3, 3), (4, 4), (5, 5), (6, 10), (6, 17), (6, 18)]:
        bad = bad_colourings_upper_bound(n, k)
        tot = 2 ** comb(n, 2)
        print(f"{k:>3} {n:>4} {bad:>24} {tot:>26} {str(bad < tot):>7}")
    print()
    print("The arithmetic engine  2^(k+2) < (k!)^2  (equivalently 2*2^(k/2) < k!):")
    for k in range(3, 10):
        lhs, rhs, ok = arithmetic_engine(k)
        print(f"   k={k}: 2^(k+2) = {lhs:<10} (k!)^2 = {rhs:<14} holds: {ok}")
    print()
    print("Largest n certified by the union bound, versus floor(2^(k/2)):")
    for k in range(3, 13):
        n_star = largest_n_by_union_bound(k)
        sqrt_bound = int(2 ** (k / 2))
        print(f"   k={k:<3} union bound gives R(k,k) > {n_star:<6} "
              f"(2^(k/2) = {sqrt_bound})")
    print()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The deletion method
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def deletion_bound_holds(n: int, k: int, t: int) -> bool:
    """The averaging hypothesis 2*C(n,k) < (t+1)*2^C(k,2) of the deletion method."""
    return 2 * comb(n, k) < (t + 1) * 2 ** comb(k, 2)


def best_deletion_bound(k: int, t_max: int = 2000) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Best (n, t, n-t) for which the deletion method certifies R(k,k) > n-t."""
    best = (0, 0, 0)
    for t in range(t_max + 1):
        n = k
        while deletion_bound_holds(n + 1, k, t):
            n += 1
        if n - t > best[2]:
            best = (n, t, n - t)
    return best


def demo_deletion() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("2. THE DELETION METHOD, AND A VERIFIED GAIN AT k = 6")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("Averaging: if 2*C(n,k) < (t+1)*2^C(k,2), some colouring has at most t")
    print("monochromatic k-sets; delete the minimum vertex of each, so R(k,k) > n-t.")
    print()
    k = 6
    print(f"   union bound at n=18, k=6: 2*C(18,6) = {2*comb(18,6)}, "
          f"2^C(6,2) = {2**comb(6,2)}  -> fails")
    print(f"   deletion at n=19, t=1  : 2*C(19,6) = {2*comb(19,6)}, "
          f"2*2^C(6,2) = {2*2**comb(6,2)}  -> holds")
    print(f"   conclusion: R(6,6) > 19 - 1 = 18")
    print()
    print("Best certificate per k (union bound t=0 versus optimised deletion):")
    print(f"{'k':>3} {'union: R > ':>14} {'deletion: R > ':>16} {'n':>7} {'t':>7}")
    for k in range(4, 13):
        u = largest_n_by_union_bound(k)
        n, t, val = best_deletion_bound(k)
        print(f"{k:>3} {u:>14} {val:>16} {n:>7} {t:>7}")
    print()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. The Ramsey sandwich
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def demo_sandwich() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("3. THE RAMSEY SANDWICH  2^(k/2) < R(k,k) <= 4^(k-1)")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("Lower: counting/deletion.  Upper: Erdos-Szekeres, R(k,k) <= C(2k-2,k-1) <= 4^(k-1).")
    print()
    print(f"{'k':>3} {'2^(k/2)':>14} {'C(2k-2,k-1)':>16} {'4^(k-1)':>16}")
    for k in range(3, 13):
        print(f"{k:>3} {2 ** (k / 2):>14.2f} {comb(2 * k - 2, k - 1):>16} "
              f"{4 ** (k - 1):>16}")
    print()
    print("Sanity check C(2m,m) <= 4^m:")
    for m in range(0, 8):
        print(f"   m={m}: C(2m,m) = {comb(2*m, m):<8} <= 4^m = {4**m}")
    print()


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Caro-Wei by greedy deletion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def caro_wei_sum(g: Graph) -> float:
    """The Caro-Wei quantity sum_v 1/(deg v + 1)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (len(nbrs) + 1) for nbrs in g.values())


def greedy_independent_set(g: Graph) -> List[int]:
    """
    Minimum-degree greedy deletion: repeatedly take a vertex of minimum degree
    inside the surviving set, output it, and delete its closed neighbourhood.
    This is the de-randomised random-permutation proof of Caro-Wei; the set it
    returns has size at least sum_v 1/(deg v + 1).
    """
    remaining: Set[int] = set(g.keys())
    chosen: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        v = min(remaining, key=lambda u: len(g[u] & remaining))
        chosen.append(v)
        remaining -= ({v} | g[v])
    return sorted(chosen)


def demo_caro_wei() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("4. CARO-WEI BY MINIMUM-DEGREE GREEDY DELETION")
    print("=" * 74)
    print("alpha(G) >= sum_v 1/(deg v + 1) >= n/(Delta+1),  and  alpha >= n^2/(2m+n).")
    print()
    examples: List[Tuple[str, Graph]] = [
        ("C_4 = T(4,2)", turan_graph(4, 2)),
        ("C_5", make_graph(5, [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 0)])),
        ("Petersen", make_graph(10,
            [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 4), (4, 0),
             (5, 7), (7, 9), (9, 6), (6, 8), (8, 5),
             (0, 5), (1, 6), (2, 7), (3, 8), (4, 9)])),
        ("K_{3,3}", make_graph(6, [(i, j) for i in range(3) for j in range(3, 6)])),
        ("T(7,3)", turan_graph(7, 3)),
        ("path P_6", make_graph(6, [(i, i + 1) for i in range(5)])),
    ]
    header = (f"{'graph':>14} {'n':>3} {'m':>4} {'CW sum':>9} {'n/(D+1)':>9} "
              f"{'n^2/(2m+n)':>11} {'greedy':>7} {'alpha':>6}")
    print(header)
    for name, g in examples:
        n, m = len(g), num_edges(g)
        delta = max(degrees(g).values()) if n else 0
        cw = caro_wei_sum(g)
        greedy = len(greedy_independent_set(g))
        alpha = independence_number(g)
        print(f"{name:>14} {n:>3} {m:>4} {cw:>9.3f} {n/(delta+1):>9.3f} "
              f"{n*n/(2*m+n):>11.3f} {greedy:>7} {alpha:>6}")
        assert greedy >= cw - 1e-9, "greedy must meet the Caro-Wei bound"

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Turan: exact counts
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def turan_edges(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """Edge count of T(n,r) from the closed-form class sizes."""
    q, s = divmod(n, r)
    sizes = [q + 1] * s + [q] * (r - s)
    return (n * n - sum(c * c for c in sizes)) // 2


def turan_identity_check(n: int, r: int) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """Verify 2*r*e(T(n,r)) + s*(r-s) = (r-1)*n^2 with s = n mod r."""
    s = n % r
    lhs = 2 * r * turan_edges(n, r) + s * (r - s)
    rhs = (r - 1) * n * n
    return lhs, rhs, lhs == rhs


def turan_extremal_number(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """ex(n, K_{r+1}) = ((r-1)n^2 - s(r-s)) / (2r)."""
    s = n % r
    return ((r - 1) * n * n - s * (r - s)) // (2 * r)


def brute_force_extremal(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """Maximum edge count of a K_{r+1}-free graph on n vertices (tiny n only)."""
    pairs = list(combinations(range(n), 2))
    best = 0
    for mask in range(1 << len(pairs)):
        edges = [pairs[i] for i in range(len(pairs)) if mask >> i & 1]
        if len(edges) <= best:
            continue
        g = make_graph(n, edges)
        if not any(all(v in g[u] for u, v in combinations(cl, 2))
                   for cl in combinations(range(n), r + 1)):
            best = len(edges)
    return best

# 6. MAX-CUT
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def cut_size(g: Graph, side: FrozenSet[int]) -> int:
    """Number of edges with exactly one endpoint in `side`."""
    return sum(1 for u in g for v in g[u] if u < v
               and ((u in side) != (v in side)))


def average_cut(g: Graph) -> float:
    """Average cut over all 2^n bipartitions; equals m/2 exactly."""
    n = len(g)
    total = 0
    for bits in product([0, 1], repeat=n):
        side = frozenset(v for v in range(n) if bits[v])
        total += cut_size(g, side)
    return total / 2 ** n


def local_search_maxcut(g: Graph) -> Tuple[FrozenSet[int], int, int]:
    """
    Local search: while some single-vertex flip increases the cut, perform it.
    Returns the final side, its cut, and the number of improving steps taken.
    Guaranteed: at most m steps, and final cut >= m/2.
    """
    side: Set[int] = set()
    steps = 0
    improved = True
    while improved:
        improved = False
        current = cut_size(g, frozenset(side))
        for v in g:
            trial = set(side)
            trial.symmetric_difference_update({v})
            if cut_size(g, frozenset(trial)) > current:
                side = trial
                steps += 1
                improved = True
                break
    return frozenset(side), cut_size(g, frozenset(side)), steps


def max_cut_exhaustive(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Maximum cut by exhaustive search over all 2^n subsets."""
    n = len(g)
    return max(cut_size(g, frozenset(v for v in range(n) if bits[v]))
               for bits in product([0, 1], repeat=n))

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. The Lovasz Local Lemma in a finite weighted space
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Clause = Tuple[Tuple[int, bool], ...]  # (variable index, required truth value)


def clause_violated(clause: Clause, assignment: Sequence[bool]) -> bool:
    """A clause is violated when every literal is false."""
    return all(assignment[var] != want for var, want in clause)


def lll_symmetric_certificate(k: int, max_shared: int) -> Tuple[float, int, float, bool]:
    """
    For a k-CNF formula in which each clause shares a variable with at most
    `max_shared` other clauses, each bad event (clause violated) has probability
    p = 2^-k under the uniform distribution and dependency degree d = max_shared.
    Returns (p, d, e*p*(d+1), whether the symmetric condition e p (d+1) <= 1 holds).
    """
    p = 2.0 ** (-k)
    d = max_shared
    value = exp(1.0) * p * (d + 1)
    return p, d, value, value <= 1.0


def search_avoiding(num_vars: int, clauses: Sequence[Clause]) -> Tuple[bool, Tuple[bool, ...]]:
    """
    Exhaustive search of the finite sample space {0,1}^num_vars for a point
    avoiding all bad events (i.e. a satisfying assignment).  The Local Lemma is
    exactly the certificate that this search never fails.
    """
    for bits in product([False, True], repeat=num_vars):
        if not any(clause_violated(c, bits) for c in clauses):
            return True, bits
    return False, ()


def dependency_degree(clauses: Sequence[Clause]) -> int:
    """Maximum number of other clauses sharing a variable with a given clause."""
    best = 0
    for i, ci in enumerate(clauses):
        vi = {v for v, _ in ci}
        best = max(best, sum(1 for j, cj in enumerate(clauses)
                             if j != i and vi & {v for v, _ in cj}))
    return best

Graph = Dict[int, Set[int]]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Small graph utilities
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def make_graph(n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Build an adjacency-set graph on vertices 0..n-1."""
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        if u == v:
            continue
        g[u].add(v)
        g[v].add(u)
    return g


def num_edges(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Number of edges of a simple graph."""
    return sum(len(nbrs) for nbrs in g.values()) // 2


def degrees(g: Graph) -> Dict[int, int]:
    """Degree of every vertex."""
    return {v: len(nbrs) for v, nbrs in g.items()}


def turan_graph(n: int, r: int) -> Graph:
    """T(n, r): vertices 0..n-1, adjacent iff their residues mod r differ."""
    return make_graph(n, [(u, v) for u in range(n) for v in range(u + 1, n)
                          if u % r != v % r])


def complement(g: Graph) -> Graph:
    """The complement graph."""
    n = len(g)
    return make_graph(n, [(u, v) for u in range(n) for v in range(u + 1, n)
                          if v not in g[u]])


def independence_number(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Exact independence number by exhaustive search (small graphs only)."""
    n = len(g)
    best = 0
    for size in range(n, 0, -1):
        if size <= best:
            break
        for s in combinations(range(n), size):
            if all(v not in g[u] for u, v in combinations(s, 2)):
                return size
    return best

# 1. Erdos' Ramsey lower bound as pure counting

def union_bound_holds(n: int, k: int) -> bool:
    """The counting hypothesis 2*C(n,k) < 2^C(k,2) of the union bound."""
    return 2 * comb(n, k) < 2 ** comb(k, 2)


def bad_colourings_upper_bound(n: int, k: int) -> int:
    """Upper bound on the number of colourings monochromatic on some k-set."""
    return comb(n, k) * 2 * 2 ** (comb(n, 2) - comb(k, 2))


def arithmetic_engine(k: int) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """The inequality 2^(k+2) < (k!)^2, valid for every k >= 3."""
    return 2 ** (k + 2), factorial(k) ** 2, 2 ** (k + 2) < factorial(k) ** 2


def largest_n_by_union_bound(k: int) -> int:
    """Largest n for which the union bound certifies R(k,k) > n."""
    n = k
    while union_bound_holds(n + 1, k):
        n += 1
    return n

def deletion_bound_holds(n: int, k: int, t: int) -> bool:
    """The averaging hypothesis 2*C(n,k) < (t+1)*2^C(k,2) of the deletion method."""
    return 2 * comb(n, k) < (t + 1) * 2 ** comb(k, 2)


def best_deletion_bound(k: int, t_max: int = 2000) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Best (n, t, n-t) for which the deletion method certifies R(k,k) > n-t."""
    best = (0, 0, 0)
    for t in range(t_max + 1):
        n = k
        while deletion_bound_holds(n + 1, k, t):
            n += 1
        if n - t > best[2]:
            best = (n, t, n - t)
    return best

# 4. Caro-Wei by greedy deletion
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def caro_wei_sum(g: Graph) -> float:
    """The Caro-Wei quantity sum_v 1/(deg v + 1)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (len(nbrs) + 1) for nbrs in g.values())


def greedy_independent_set(g: Graph) -> List[int]:
    """
    Minimum-degree greedy deletion: repeatedly take a vertex of minimum degree
    inside the surviving set, output it, and delete its closed neighbourhood.
    This is the de-randomised random-permutation proof of Caro-Wei; the set it
    returns has size at least sum_v 1/(deg v + 1).
    """
    remaining: Set[int] = set(g.keys())
    chosen: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        v = min(remaining, key=lambda u: len(g[u] & remaining))
        chosen.append(v)
        remaining -= ({v} | g[v])
    return sorted(chosen)

# 5. Turan: exact counts

def turan_edges(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """Edge count of T(n,r) from the closed-form class sizes."""
    q, s = divmod(n, r)
    sizes = [q + 1] * s + [q] * (r - s)
    return (n * n - sum(c * c for c in sizes)) // 2


def turan_identity_check(n: int, r: int) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """Verify 2*r*e(T(n,r)) + s*(r-s) = (r-1)*n^2 with s = n mod r."""
    s = n % r
    lhs = 2 * r * turan_edges(n, r) + s * (r - s)
    rhs = (r - 1) * n * n
    return lhs, rhs, lhs == rhs


def turan_extremal_number(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """ex(n, K_{r+1}) = ((r-1)n^2 - s(r-s)) / (2r)."""
    s = n % r
    return ((r - 1) * n * n - s * (r - s)) // (2 * r)


def brute_force_extremal(n: int, r: int) -> int:
    """Maximum edge count of a K_{r+1}-free graph on n vertices (tiny n only)."""
    pairs = list(combinations(range(n), 2))
    best = 0
    for mask in range(1 << len(pairs)):
        edges = [pairs[i] for i in range(len(pairs)) if mask >> i & 1]
        if len(edges) <= best:
            continue
        g = make_graph(n, edges)
        if not any(all(v in g[u] for u, v in combinations(cl, 2))
                   for cl in combinations(range(n), r + 1)):
            best = len(edges)
    return best

# 6. MAX-CUT

def cut_size(g: Graph, side: FrozenSet[int]) -> int:
    """Number of edges with exactly one endpoint in `side`."""
    return sum(1 for u in g for v in g[u] if u < v
               and ((u in side) != (v in side)))


def average_cut(g: Graph) -> float:
    """Average cut over all 2^n bipartitions; equals m/2 exactly."""
    n = len(g)
    total = 0
    for bits in product([0, 1], repeat=n):
        side = frozenset(v for v in range(n) if bits[v])
        total += cut_size(g, side)
    return total / 2 ** n


def local_search_maxcut(g: Graph) -> Tuple[FrozenSet[int], int, int]:
    """
    Local search: while some single-vertex flip increases the cut, perform it.
    Returns the final side, its cut, and the number of improving steps taken.
    Guaranteed: at most m steps, and final cut >= m/2.
    """
    side: Set[int] = set()
    steps = 0
    improved = True
    while improved:
        improved = False
        current = cut_size(g, frozenset(side))
        for v in g:
            trial = set(side)
            trial.symmetric_difference_update({v})
            if cut_size(g, frozenset(trial)) > current:
                side = trial
                steps += 1
                improved = True
                break
    return frozenset(side), cut_size(g, frozenset(side)), steps


def max_cut_exhaustive(g: Graph) -> int:
    """Maximum cut by exhaustive search over all 2^n subsets."""
    n = len(g)
    return max(cut_size(g, frozenset(v for v in range(n) if bits[v]))
               for bits in product([0, 1], repeat=n))

# 7. The Lovasz Local Lemma in a finite weighted space
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Clause = Tuple[Tuple[int, bool], ...]  # (variable index, required truth value)


def clause_violated(clause: Clause, assignment: Sequence[bool]) -> bool:
    """A clause is violated when every literal is false."""
    return all(assignment[var] != want for var, want in clause)


def lll_symmetric_certificate(k: int, max_shared: int) -> Tuple[float, int, float, bool]:
    """
    For a k-CNF formula in which each clause shares a variable with at most
    `max_shared` other clauses, each bad event (clause violated) has probability
    p = 2^-k under the uniform distribution and dependency degree d = max_shared.
    Returns (p, d, e*p*(d+1), whether the symmetric condition e p (d+1) <= 1 holds).
    """
    p = 2.0 ** (-k)
    d = max_shared
    value = exp(1.0) * p * (d + 1)
    return p, d, value, value <= 1.0


def search_avoiding(num_vars: int, clauses: Sequence[Clause]) -> Tuple[bool, Tuple[bool, ...]]:
    """
    Exhaustive search of the finite sample space {0,1}^num_vars for a point
    avoiding all bad events (i.e. a satisfying assignment).  The Local Lemma is
    exactly the certificate that this search never fails.
    """
    for bits in product([False, True], repeat=num_vars):
        if not any(clause_violated(c, bits) for c in clauses):
            return True, bits
    return False, ()


def dependency_degree(clauses: Sequence[Clause]) -> int:
    """Maximum number of other clauses sharing a variable with a given clause."""
    best = 0
    for i, ci in enumerate(clauses):
        vi = {v for v, _ in ci}
        best = max(best, sum(1 for j, cj in enumerate(clauses)
                             if j != i and vi & {v for v, _ in cj}))
    return best

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Dict, Iterable, List, Set, Tuple

Graph = Dict[int, Set[int]]


def build_graph(n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Adjacency-set representation of a simple graph on 0..n-1."""
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:
        if u != v:
            g[u].add(v)
            g[v].add(u)
    return g


def caro_wei_bound(g: Graph) -> float:
    """The guaranteed size sum_v 1/(deg v + 1)."""
    return sum(1.0 / (len(nb) + 1) for nb in g.values())


def greedy_independent_set(g: Graph) -> List[int]:
    """
    Repeatedly select a vertex of minimum degree *inside the surviving set*,
    add it to the output, and delete its closed neighbourhood.

    Guarantee (Caro-Wei): the returned set is independent and has size at least
    sum_v 1/(deg v + 1), hence at least n/(Delta+1) and at least n^2/(2m+n).
    """
    remaining: Set[int] = set(g)
    chosen: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        v = min(remaining, key=lambda u: len(g[u] & remaining))
        chosen.append(v)
        remaining -= ({v} | g[v])
    return sorted(chosen)


def certify(g: Graph) -> Tuple[List[int], float, bool, bool]:
    """Run the algorithm and check independence and the Caro-Wei guarantee."""
    s = greedy_independent_set(g)
    bound = caro_wei_bound(g)
    independent = all(b not in g[a] for i, a in enumerate(s) for b in s[i + 1:])
    return s, bound, independent, len(s) >= bound - 1e-12

minimum vertex of each such set, and restrict the colouring to what remains.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import comb
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple


def averaging_condition(n: int, k: int, t: int) -> bool:
    """2*C(n,k) < (t+1) * 2^C(k,2): some colouring has at most t bad k-sets."""
    return 2 * comb(n, k) < (t + 1) * 2 ** comb(k, 2)


def largest_n(k: int, t: int) -> int:
    """Largest n satisfying the averaging condition for this t."""
    n = k
    while averaging_condition(n + 1, k, t):
        n += 1
    return n


def best_deletion_certificate(k: int, t_max: int = 4000) -> Tuple[int, int, int]:
    """Maximise n - t over t <= t_max; returns (n, t, bound) with R(k,k) > bound."""
    best = (k, 0, 0)
    for t in range(t_max + 1):
        n = largest_n(k, t)
        if n - t > best[2]:
            best = (n, t, n - t)
    return best


def minimum_element_transversal(bad_sets: Iterable[FrozenSet[int]]) -> Set[int]:
    """
    The explicit deletion set: the minimum element of every bad set.  It meets
    every bad set and has at most as many elements as there are bad sets, so no
    choice principle is needed.
    """
    return {min(s) for s in bad_sets if s}


def monochromatic_sets(n: int, k: int, red: Set[FrozenSet[int]]) -> List[FrozenSet[int]]:
    """All k-subsets of {0..n-1} on which the colouring `red` is monochromatic."""
    from itertools import combinations
    out: List[FrozenSet[int]] = []
    for kset in combinations(range(n), k):
        pairs = [frozenset(p) for p in combinations(kset, 2)]
        if all(p in red for p in pairs) or all(p not in red for p in pairs):
            out.append(frozenset(kset))
    return out


def delete_and_restrict(n: int, k: int, red: Set[FrozenSet[int]]
                        ) -> Tuple[List[int], Set[FrozenSet[int]], int]:
    """
    Apply the deletion step to an explicit colouring: compute its monochromatic
    k-sets, delete the minimum vertex of each, and restrict the colouring to the
    surviving vertices.  Returns (survivors, restricted colouring, #deleted).
    """
    bad = monochromatic_sets(n, k, red)
    kill = minimum_element_transversal(bad)
    survivors = [v for v in range(n) if v not in kill]
    keep = set(survivors)
    restricted = {e for e in red if set(e) <= keep}
    return survivors, restricted, len(kill)

def clause_violated(clause: Clause, x: Assignment) -> bool:

def make_graph(n: int, edges: Iterable[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Graph:
    """Adjacency-set graph on vertices 0..n-1."""
    g: Graph = {v: set() for v in range(n)}
    for u, v in edges:

            g[u].add(v)
            g[v].add(u)

    """sum_v 1/(deg v + 1)."""

def greedy_independent_set(g: Graph) -> List[int]:
    """Minimum-degree greedy deletion."""
    remaining: Set[int] = set(g)
    out: List[int] = []
    while remaining:
        v = min(remaining, key=lambda u: len(g[u] & remaining))
        out.append(v)
        remaining -= ({v} | g[v])
    return out

    """Exact independence number (exhaustive; small graphs only)."""

    return 0

<p class="lede">
Colour every pair of <em>n</em> people red or blue. A colouring is just a <em>subset</em> of the
pair set, so there are exactly 2<sup>C(n,2)</sup> of them. The colourings that are monochromatic on
a fixed group of <em>k</em> people number 2·2<sup>C(n,2)−C(k,2)</sup>, so at most
C(n,k)·2·2<sup>C(n,2)−C(k,2)</sup> are bad overall. When that is smaller than the total,
a good colouring must exist — no probability required. The deletion refinement goes further:
if the <em>average</em> number of bad groups is below <em>t</em>+1, some colouring has at most <em>t</em>

*A guided tour of the probabilistic method, rebuilt out of nothing but counting.*

---

## 0. The question that started it all

In 1947 Paul Erdős asked how large a party must be before you can guarantee $k$ mutual friends or $k$ mutual strangers. Call that number $R(k,k)$. Rather than *build* a party avoiding both — nobody knows how — he flipped a coin for every pair and argued that a random party works with positive probability.

That is the **probabilistic method**, and its reputation is that it is *non-constructive*: it proves the needle is in the haystack without pointing at it.

This page takes that reputation apart. Every argument below starts as a statement about random objects and ends as a statement about **integers, greedy choices, or local moves** — with an algorithm attached.

<details>
<summary><b>Background: what exactly is a Ramsey number?</b> (click to expand)</summary>

Colour every edge of the complete graph $K_n$ red or blue. A *monochromatic $K_k$* is a set of $k$ vertices all of whose $\binom{k}{2}$ internal edges get the same colour. [Ramsey's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsey%27s_theorem) (1930) says that for each $k$ there is a finite $n$ forcing a monochromatic $K_k$; the least such $n$ is $R(k,k)$.

Known values are tiny: $R(3,3)=6$, $R(4,4)=18$, and $R(5,5)$ is still unknown (it lies between $43$ and $46$). Erdős famously said that if aliens demanded $R(5,5)$ we should marshal all our computers; if they demanded $R(6,6)$ we should attack them instead.
</details>

---

## 1. Probability is a fraction: colourings are just subsets

Here is the entire trick. **A two-colouring of $K_n$ is a subset of the pair set** — the set of red edges. There are exactly $2^{\binom{n}{2}}$ of them.

Now fix a group $K$ of $k$ vertices, with $\binom{k}{2}$ internal pairs.

* The colourings that make all of $K$'s pairs red are the subsets containing a fixed $\binom{k}{2}$-element set: there are $2^{\binom{n}{2}-\binom{k}{2}}$ of them.
* The colourings that make all of $K$'s pairs blue are the subsets *disjoint* from that same set: again $2^{\binom{n}{2}-\binom{k}{2}}$.

Add them, sum over the $\binom{n}{k}$ groups, and you get the whole "probabilistic" argument as a comparison of integers:

$$\underbrace{\binom{n}{k}\cdot 2\cdot 2^{\binom{n}{2}-\binom{k}{2}}}_{\text{bad colourings, at most}} \;<\; \underbrace{2^{\binom{n}{2}}}_{\text{all colourings}} \iff 2\binom{n}{k} < 2^{\binom{k}{2}}.$$

If the inequality holds, a good colouring exists — because a family strictly smaller than the whole cannot be the whole.

Play with the two sides yourself. Watch the moment the union bound fails (try $k=6$, $n=18$), then discover what the deletion trick buys you.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why "positive probability" and "not all of them" are the same sentence</b></summary>

Under the uniform measure on the $2^{\binom{n}{2}}$ colourings, $\mathbb{P}[\text{bad}] = \dfrac{\#\text{bad}}{2^{\binom n2}}$. So

$$\mathbb{P}[\text{bad}] < 1 \iff \#\text{bad} < 2^{\binom n2}.$$

Probability adds nothing here except vocabulary. In a **finite** space, "an event has positive probability" is literally "the event is a non-empty set", and every union bound is the subadditivity of cardinality: $|A\cup B|\le |A|+|B|$.
</details>

## 2. The arithmetic that makes $2^{k/2}$ appear

The counting condition $2\binom{n}{k}<2^{\binom k2}$ becomes the familiar $R(k,k)>2^{k/2}$ through one elementary inequality:

> **Lemma.** For every $k \ge 3$: $\;2^{k+2} < (k!)^2$, equivalently $2\cdot 2^{k/2} < k!$.

Base case $k=3$: $32 < 36$. Step: the left side doubles while the right side multiplies by $(k+1)^2 \ge 16$.

Bounding $\binom{n}{k}\le n^k/k!$ and using $n^2 \le 2^k$, this is exactly enough to push the counting condition through, giving:

> **Theorem (Erdős, 1947).** If $3 \le k \le n$ and $n \le 2^{k/2}$, there is a graph on $n$ vertices such that neither it nor its complement has a clique of size $k$. Hence $R(k,k) > 2^{k/2}$.

On the other side, the [Erdős–Szekeres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Szekeres_theorem) recursion gives $R(k,k)\le\binom{2k-2}{k-1}\le 4^{k-1}$, so the truth is caught in a sandwich:

$$2^{k/2} \;<\; R(k,k) \;\le\; 4^{k-1}.$$

Eighty years on, nobody has improved either exponent by more than lower-order factors.

{{visualization:1}}

## 3. Deleting instead of discarding

Erdős's union bound is wasteful: a colouring with a *single* monochromatic $k$-set is thrown away entirely. The **deletion method** keeps it and removes one vertex instead.

Sum the number of monochromatic $k$-sets over *all* colourings; by symmetry this double count equals $2\binom{n}{k}2^{\binom n2 - \binom k2}$, so the average colouring has $2\binom nk / 2^{\binom k2}$ bad sets. If that average is below $t+1$, some colouring has at most $t$ of them.

> **Theorem (deletion).** If $2\binom{n}{k} < (t+1)2^{\binom{k}{2}}$, then $R(k,k) > n - t$.

The deletion step needs no choice principle: **take the minimum-numbered vertex of each bad set**. That transversal is explicit, has at most $t$ elements, and meets every bad set.

The concrete payoff at $k=6$: the union bound already fails at $n=18$ (since $2\binom{18}{6}=37128 \ge 32768 = 2^{15}$), but at $n=19$ we have $2\binom{19}{6}=54264 < 2\cdot 32768$, so one deletion gives a good colouring on $18$ vertices: $R(6,6)>18$.

{{algorithm:1}}

## 4. The star of the show: a random permutation collapses into greed

Now the most striking de-randomisation. The **Caro–Wei inequality** says every graph has an independent set of size at least

$$\sum_{v} \frac{1}{\deg(v)+1}.$$

Classical proof: shuffle the vertices uniformly at random, keep each vertex that precedes all of its neighbours. Vertex $v$ is kept exactly when it is first among the $\deg(v)+1$ members of its closed neighbourhood — probability $1/(\deg(v)+1)$ — and linearity of expectation does the rest.

De-randomised proof: **run the greedy algorithm.** Take a vertex of minimum degree, keep it, delete its closed neighbourhood, repeat.

Try it. Build any graph you like, then step through the algorithm and watch the guarantee being paid off one block at a time.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the full proof (it is three lines of bookkeeping)</b></summary>

The trick is to *relativise*: for a surviving set $t$, write $\deg_t(v)$ for the number of neighbours of $v$ inside $t$. We prove by strong induction on $|t|$:

> for every $t$ there is an independent $s \subseteq t$ with $\sum_{v\in t} \frac{1}{\deg_t(v)+1} \le |s|$.

Pick $v \in t$ of minimum relative degree $d$, and let $B$ be its closed neighbourhood inside $t$, so $|B| = d+1$.

1. **The block $B$ costs at most $1$.** Every $u \in B$ has $\deg_t(u)\ge d$ by minimality, so each term is at most $\frac{1}{d+1}$, and there are $d+1$ of them.
2. **The rest only improves.** For $u \in t\setminus B$, deleting vertices cannot raise a degree: $\deg_{t\setminus B}(u)\le \deg_t(u)$, so its term in the sum over $t$ is at most its term in the sum over $t\setminus B$, which the induction hypothesis already pays for with an independent set $s'$.
3. **Adding $v$ is free.** All of $v$'s neighbours were deleted with $B$, so $\{v\}\cup s'$ is independent, and $|s'|+1$ covers $\left(\sum_{t\setminus B}\right) + 1$.

Taking $t = V$ gives Caro–Wei. Note what happened: the random permutation vanished, and what remains is a linear-time algorithm that is *easier* than the probabilistic argument.
</details>

{{algorithm:0}}

The inequality is a workhorse. Two immediate corollaries:

* Since $\deg(v)\le\Delta$ for all $v$: $\;\alpha(G) \ge \dfrac{n}{\Delta+1}$.
* By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in Sedrakyan's form $\sum_v 1/a_v \ge n^2/\sum_v a_v$ with $a_v = \deg(v)+1$, and the handshake identity $\sum_v \deg(v)=2m$: $\;\alpha(G)\ge \dfrac{n^2}{2m+n}$.

And one that looks like it belongs to a different subject entirely: in a **triangle-free** graph every neighbourhood is independent, so $\Delta \le \alpha$, whence $n \le \alpha(\alpha+1)$. Contrapositively, every graph on more than $k(k+1)$ vertices has a triangle or an independent set of size $k+1$ — an off-diagonal Ramsey bound $R(3,k+1)>k^2$, obtained with no probability at all.

## 5. Turán's theorem, upside down and exact

Apply Caro–Wei to the **complement**. A graph with no clique of size $r+1$ has $\alpha(G^c)\le r$, and $\sum_v(\deg_{G^c}(v)+1) = n^2-2m$, so Sedrakyan gives

$$\frac{n^2}{n^2-2m} \le \sum_v \frac{1}{\deg_{G^c}(v)+1} \le \alpha(G^c) \le r \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m \le \Bigl(1-\frac1r\Bigr)\frac{n^2}{2}.$$

That is **Turán's theorem**, with no divisibility hypothesis anywhere.

But is the bound attained? The extremal graph is the Turán graph $T(n,r)$ — $r$ classes, as equal as possible, all cross pairs joined — and here the counting viewpoint pays an unexpected dividend. Counting the classes exactly, with $s = n \bmod r$:

$$2r\,e\bigl(T(n,r)\bigr) + s(r-s) = (r-1)n^2, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad e\bigl(T(n,r)\bigr) = \Bigl(1-\frac1r\Bigr)\frac{n^2}{2} - \frac{s(r-s)}{2r}.$$

So the clean value is attained **exactly when $r \mid n$**, and the true extremal number is

$$\mathrm{ex}(n,K_{r+1}) = \frac{(r-1)n^2 - s(r-s)}{2r}.$$

Textbooks often say you may simply round the clean value down. That is true precisely when $s(r-s) < 2r$ — and it is **false** in general. Find the first counterexample yourself: the heat map below turns red exactly where rounding down overshoots.

{{interactive_demo:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>The counterexample, spelled out: $n=12$, $r=8$</b></summary>

With $n=12$ and $r=8$ we get $s = 12 \bmod 8 = 4$, so the classes are $2,2,2,2,1,1,1,1$ and

$$2\cdot 12^2 = 288, \qquad \sum_i |C_i|^2 = 4\cdot 4 + 4\cdot 1 = 20, \qquad e = \frac{144-20}{2} = 62.$$

Meanwhile $\left\lfloor \left(1-\tfrac18\right)\tfrac{144}{2}\right\rfloor = \lfloor 63 \rfloor = 63$. The deficit is $s(r-s)/(2r) = 16/16 = 1$, exactly enough to make rounding down wrong. For every modulus $r < 8$ the floor formula is correct for all $n$; $r = 8$ is where it first breaks.
</details>

## 6. When the union bound is hopeless: the Local Lemma

Suppose you have a million bad events, each of probability $1/100$. The union bound is useless. But if each event depends on only a couple of others, the **[Lovász Local Lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lov%C3%A1sz_local_lemma)** rescues you:

> **Theorem (symmetric form).** If every bad event has probability at most $p$, every event's dependency neighbourhood has at most $d$ members (with the one-sided independence bound holding outside it), and
> $$e\,p\,(d+1)\le 1,$$
> then some outcome avoids all the bad events simultaneously.

Notice the hypothesis contains no $n$ at all. Locality, not size, is what matters.

The setting we use is a **finite weighted probability space**: a finite set of outcomes with nonnegative weights summing to $1$. That is a purely finitary object — and so the conclusion "the good event has positive probability" says exactly "the good set is non-empty". Hence:

> **The existence proof is a termination certificate.** Enumerate the outcomes and return the first one avoiding all bad events. This search is sound by construction, and the Local Lemma guarantees it never fails.

{{algorithm:3}}

<details>
<summary><b>The Erdős–Lovász double induction, sketched</b></summary>

One proves, for every index $i$ and every set $S$ of indices with $i\notin S$,

$$\mathbb{P}\Bigl(A_i \cap \bigcap_{j\in S}\overline{A_j}\Bigr) \le x_i\,\mathbb{P}\Bigl(\bigcap_{j\in S}\overline{A_j}\Bigr),$$

by induction on $|S|$. Split $S$ into $S_1 = S \cap \Gamma(i)$ (the dependent part) and $S_2 = S\setminus\Gamma(i)$ (the independent part). Bound the numerator using independence from $S_2$; bound the denominator from below by $\prod_{j\in S_1}(1-x_j)$ times the same quantity, peeling one index of $S_1$ at a time via the induction hypothesis. The weight condition $\mathbb{P}(A_i)\le x_i\prod_{j\in\Gamma(i)}(1-x_j)$ then converts the ratio into $x_i$.

Peeling all indices gives $\mathbb{P}\left(\bigcap_i \overline{A_i}\right)\ge \prod_i (1-x_i) > 0$. The symmetric version sets every $x_i = 1/(d+1)$ and uses $\left(1-\tfrac{1}{d+1}\right)^{d}\ge e^{-1}$, which is just $1+x\le e^x$ in disguise.
</details>

This is the weakest useful form of constructivity — the search is exponential. Making it *efficient* is the content of the Moser–Tardos resampling algorithm: repeatedly resample the variables of a currently violated event. Its analysis (entropy compression, witness trees) is itself a counting argument, so it belongs in this same finitary world.

## 7. Local search: the friendliest de-randomisation of all

**MAX-CUT**: split the vertices into two sides so as to cut as many edges as possible. The probabilistic proof that half the edges can always be cut is one line — each vertex goes to a random side, each edge is cut with probability $1/2$.

Two de-randomisations, both exact:

1. **Averaging.** Summing the cut size over *all* $2^n$ bipartitions gives exactly $2m\cdot 2^{n-2}$, so the average is $m/2$; some subset achieves it, and exhaustive search finds one.
2. **Local search.** Flipping a single vertex $v$ changes the cut by exactly $\deg(v) - 2c_S(v)$, where $c_S(v)$ counts $v$'s edges already crossing. So at a *locally maximal* cut, every vertex has at least half its edges cut; summing gives $m \le 2\cdot\mathrm{cut}$. And since the cut is a strictly increasing integer bounded by $m$, local search stops after at most $m$ improvements.

{{algorithm:2}}

The two families meet in a pleasing place: for the complete graph the search returns the balanced bipartition, of size $\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lceil n/2\rceil$ — which is precisely $e(T(n,2))$. **The largest bipartite subgraph of $K_n$ is the extremal triangle-free graph.**

## 8. Run everything at once

The demonstration below reproduces every number quoted on this page: the counting inequalities, the deletion gain at $k=6$, the greedy sets versus their Caro–Wei guarantees, the exact Turán identity and its counterexample, the MAX-CUT identities, and the certified Local Lemma search.

{{demo:0}}

## 9. What to take away

There are two different things people mean by "non-constructive".

* **Finitary non-constructivity** — the proof averages instead of building. This dissolves on contact: in a finite universe, positive probability means non-empty, and the argument hands you a terminating search.
* **Computational non-constructivity** — the search is exponential and no fast algorithm is known. This is real, and for Ramsey colourings it is wide open.

Between those poles lies everything interesting. Caro–Wei's random permutation becomes a near-linear greedy algorithm. MAX-CUT's random bipartition becomes a local search terminating in at most $m$ steps. Turán's theorem never needed randomness — and doing its count exactly exposed a folklore formula as wrong at $n=12$, $r=8$. Only the Ramsey bound and the Local Lemma resist, and they resist for reasons of *search-space size*, not logic.

Erdős's existence proofs were algorithms in disguise. The disguise was the word "probability".

# Bridge: hypergraph 2-colourability (property B) by the same counting engine

Erdős (1963): every `k`-uniform hypergraph with fewer than `2^{k-1}` edges is 2-colourable.
The textbook proof colours the vertices at random; the proof here is the *same* argument with
the probability replaced by cardinalities of `Finset`s — and, crucially, it reuses verbatim the
two counting lemmas `card_filter_superset` and `card_filter_disjoint` proved for the Ramsey
bound in `Bridges/ErdosProbabilisticRamsey.lean`.  That reuse is the point: the "probabilistic
method" here is one single counting engine applied to two different extremal problems.

## Main results

* `card_bad_colourings_le` : union bound — at most `#H · 2 · 2 ^ (card V - k)` colourings make
  some edge monochromatic.
* `exists_proper_two_colouring` : if `#H < 2 ^ (k-1)` then a proper 2-colouring exists.
* `property_B_sharp_example` : the bound is not vacuous and is attained in spirit — for `k = 1`
  the hypothesis `#H < 1` is exactly what is needed, since a single singleton edge is

import Mathlib
import Bridges.ErdosProbabilisticRamsey

open Finset

namespace PropertyBUnionBound

open ErdosProbabilisticRamsey (card_filter_superset card_filter_disjoint)

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- A colouring `S ⊆ V` (the "red" vertices) makes the edge `E` monochromatic when `E` is
entirely red or entirely blue. -/
def MonoEdge (S E : Finset V) : Prop := E ⊆ S ∨ Disjoint S E

instance (S E : Finset V) : Decidable (MonoEdge S E) := by unfold MonoEdge; infer_instance

/-- The colourings that make some edge of `H` monochromatic. -/
def badColourings (H : Finset (Finset V)) : Finset (Finset V) :=
  (univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => ∃ E ∈ H, MonoEdge S E)

/-- **Union bound.**  At most `#H · (2 · 2 ^ (card V - k))` colourings make some `k`-element edge
monochromatic. -/
theorem card_bad_colourings_le (H : Finset (Finset V)) (k : ℕ) (hk : ∀ E ∈ H, #E = k) :
    #(badColourings H) ≤ #H * (2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k)) := by
  classical
  have hsub : badColourings H ⊆ H.biUnion
      (fun E => (univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => MonoEdge S E)) := by
    intro S hS
    simp only [badColourings, mem_filter, mem_powerset] at hS
    obtain ⟨E, hE, hmono⟩ := hS.2
    exact mem_biUnion.2 ⟨E, hE, by simp only [mem_filter, mem_powerset]; exact ⟨hS.1, hmono⟩⟩
  have hone : ∀ E ∈ H, #((univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => MonoEdge S E)) ≤
      2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k) := by
    intro E hE
    have hEsub : E ⊆ (univ : Finset V) := subset_univ E
    have hsplit : (univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => MonoEdge S E) ⊆
        (univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => E ⊆ S) ∪
          (univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => Disjoint S E) := by
      intro S hS
      simp only [mem_filter, mem_powerset, MonoEdge] at hS
      rcases hS.2 with h | h
      · exact mem_union_left _ (by simp only [mem_filter, mem_powerset]; exact ⟨hS.1, h⟩)
      · exact mem_union_right _ (by simp only [mem_filter, mem_powerset]; exact ⟨hS.1, h⟩)
    calc #((univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => MonoEdge S E)) ≤ _ := card_le_card hsplit
      _ ≤ #((univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => E ⊆ S)) +
          #((univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => Disjoint S E)) := card_union_le _ _
      _ = 2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k) := by
          rw [card_filter_superset _ _ hEsub, card_filter_disjoint _ _ hEsub, card_univ, hk E hE]
          ring
  calc #(badColourings H) ≤ #(H.biUnion
        (fun E => (univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => MonoEdge S E))) := card_le_card hsub
    _ ≤ ∑ E ∈ H, #((univ : Finset V).powerset.filter (fun S => MonoEdge S E)) := card_biUnion_le
    _ ≤ ∑ _E ∈ H, 2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k) := sum_le_sum hone
    _ = #H * (2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k)) := by rw [sum_const, smul_eq_mul]

/-- **Erdős' property B theorem.**  A `k`-uniform hypergraph with fewer than `2 ^ (k-1)` edges
admits a 2-colouring of its vertices with no monochromatic edge. -/
theorem exists_proper_two_colouring (H : Finset (Finset V)) (k : ℕ)
    (hk : ∀ E ∈ H, #E = k) (hcard : #H < 2 ^ (k - 1)) :
    ∃ S : Finset V, ∀ E ∈ H, ¬ MonoEdge S E := by
  classical
  rcases H.eq_empty_or_nonempty with hH | ⟨E₀, hE₀⟩
  · exact ⟨∅, by simp [hH]⟩
  · -- a nonempty hypergraph forces `1 ≤ k ≤ card V`
    have hkle : k ≤ Fintype.card V := by
      have : #E₀ ≤ Fintype.card V := by
        simpa using card_le_card (subset_univ E₀)
      rwa [hk E₀ hE₀] at this
    have hk1 : 1 ≤ k := by
      rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos k with hk0 | hk0
      · exfalso
        rw [hk0] at hcard
        simp only [Nat.zero_sub, pow_zero] at hcard
        have : 0 < #H := card_pos.2 ⟨E₀, hE₀⟩
        omega
      · exact hk0
    have hbad : #(badColourings H) < 2 ^ (Fintype.card V) := by
      have h1 := card_bad_colourings_le H k hk
      have h2 : #H * (2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k)) <
          2 ^ (k - 1) * (2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k)) := by
        refine Nat.mul_lt_mul_of_lt_of_le hcard (le_refl _) ?_
        positivity
      have h3 : 2 ^ (k - 1) * (2 * 2 ^ (Fintype.card V - k)) = 2 ^ (Fintype.card V) := by
        rw [← pow_succ', ← pow_add]
        congr 1
        omega
      omega
    have hsubset : badColourings H ⊆ (univ : Finset V).powerset := filter_subset _ _
    have hne : badColourings H ≠ (univ : Finset V).powerset := by
      intro hEq
      rw [hEq, card_powerset, card_univ] at hbad
      exact lt_irrefl _ hbad
    obtain ⟨S, hS, hSbad⟩ : ∃ S ∈ (univ : Finset V).powerset, S ∉ badColourings H := by
      by_contra hcon
      push_neg at hcon
      exact hne (Finset.Subset.antisymm hsubset hcon)
    refine ⟨S, fun E hE hmono => hSbad ?_⟩
    simp only [badColourings, mem_filter, mem_powerset]
    exact ⟨mem_powerset.1 hS, E, hE, hmono⟩

omit [Fintype V] in
/-- Sharpness sanity check at `k = 1`: a hypergraph consisting of one singleton edge has
`#H = 1 = 2 ^ (1-1)`, and indeed *every* colouring makes that edge monochromatic, so the
strict inequality `#H < 2 ^ (k-1)` in `exists_proper_two_colouring` cannot be weakened to `≤`. -/
theorem property_B_sharp_example (v : V) :
    ∀ S : Finset V, MonoEdge S ({v} : Finset V) := by
  intro S
  by_cases hv : v ∈ S
  · exact Or.inl (by simpa using hv)
  · exact Or.inr (by simpa [Finset.disjoint_singleton_right] using hv)

end PropertyBUnionBound",

# Bridge: the max-cut half-of-the-edges bound, as a finite count and as a terminating search

The classical probabilistic proof that every graph has a cut containing at least half of its
edges puts every vertex on one of the two sides independently: each edge is then cut with
probability `1/2`, so the expected size of the cut is `m/2` and some cut is at least that large.

As everywhere else in this thread, the probability is replaced here by a *cardinality*: the sum
of the cut sizes over **all** `2 ^ n` subsets `S ⊆ V` is computed exactly
(`sum_cut_eq_card_adjPairs_mul`), and the existence statement is then pure pigeonhole on natural
numbers.  Finally the existence is upgraded to an explicit object: `maxCut G` is the supremum of
the cut function over the (finite, decidable) powerset — a terminating exhaustive search — and it
provably meets the bound and is attained by a concrete subset.  This is the "existence proof is an
algorithm in disguise" slogan of the mission in its smallest complete instance.

## Main results

* `card_filter_mem_notMem` : exactly `2 ^ (n - 2)` of the subsets of `V` contain `u` but not `v`.
* `sum_cut_eq_card_adjPairs_mul` : `∑_{S ⊆ V} cut S = (2 · #edges) · 2 ^ (n - 2)`, an exact
  identity — the finite form of "the expected cut is `m/2`".
* `exists_cut_ge_half_edges` : some `S` satisfies `#edges ≤ 2 · cut S`.
* `maxCut_ge_half_edges` : the exhaustive search `maxCut G` already satisfies the bound, and
  `exists_cut_eq_maxCut` shows it is attained by an explicit subset.
* `exists_bool_colouring_cut` : the same statement phrased as a `2`-colouring `f : V → Bool`.
* `maxCut_triangle`, `maxCut_completeGraph_four` : the search evaluated on `K₃` and `K₄`, showing
  the bound is tight for `K₃` (`3 ≤ 2 · 2`) and strict for `K₄` (`6 ≤ 2 · 4`).

## Catalog connections
* `Bridges/ErdosProbabilisticRamsey.lean` : the counting lemma `card_filter_superset` is reused
  verbatim to count the subsets containing a given pair.
* `Bridges/PropertyBUnionBound.lean` : the same "colourings are subsets" encoding.
